Joe Rogan thought it had to be a conspiracy theory: AI companies quietly buying millions of books, scanning them, and throwing the originals away. Then Jamie looked it up. ROGAN: "Oh my god, it's true." Anthropic had a code name for it: "Project Panama." The internal memo: "Project Panama is our effort to destructively scan all the books in the world." "We don't want it to be known that we are working on this." Rogan's reaction: "The training data is other people's work. It's books. That's what's insane." How it played out: Anthropic bought millions of books, cut off the spines, scanned every page and discarded them. Authors sued in Bartz v. Anthropic. The judge ruled the scanning of purchased books was fair use. The pirated books were another story. Anthropic had also downloaded millions from pirate sites, and that part cost it $1.5 billion, the largest copyright settlement in US history. About $3,000 per pirated book. Interested in AI? Impressive paper from CMU. Soon, we will have coding agents that can tune the entire stack, from prompts to token serving. This work experiments with coding agents to tune an LLM serving stack. They get Claude Sonnet 5.5 to build a serving system for Gemma E4B that delivers 4.87x the value per GPU dollar of the vLLM reference. ServerBench asks coding agents to design a complete, specialized serving system and decide how many concurrent sessions to run. The score is latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost, measured by replaying real coding sessions with their dependencies intact. An independent check verifies the system works. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, 22 of 33 runs produced a verified system and 13 beat the strongest baseline. The best designs raised capacity and chose the load to match it. Failed runs often shipped optimizations whose new code paths were never tested. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06841 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/serverbench-how-can-your-coding-agents-design-specialized-llm-serving-systems-2611.06841

Recommended benchmark from OpenAI on agents for everyday life tasks. They surveyed 3,837 US consumers to rank 148 life tasks by what people would pay an assistant to handle. Together, those tasks are worth over $1.7 trillion a year. LifeVal turns the most valuable of them into 169 agent tasks. Each one is written by someone who has done the task many times in real life, using their own ChatGPT conversations, memories, and files. The tasks include managing finances, moving apartments, searching for a job, and finding childcare. Every task comes with a rubric, a working environment and an offline copy of the web, and passes three rounds of human review. Scores rise steadily from GPT-5.2 to GPT-6 Astra. The most common failure for every model is a wrong answer or recommendation, often because the model missed a fact sitting in the user's past chats. On criteria tied only to past conversations, the win rate was 33%, compared with 48% for saved memories. If you build assistants with memory, test whether the agent actually finds what the user told it weeks ago. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.06687 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/lifeval-evaluating-ai-model-performance-on-personalized-agentic-consumer-tasks-2611.06687

Own your intelligence stack, folks! We've reached the point where it's simply not possible to do reliable groundbreaking AI research (using autoresearch loops) with GPT or Claude. I constantly get hammered with inaccurate refusals. This is sad! They should at least spend time fixing their classifiers. But over the last year, I've learned to build my own thing and own more of the intelligence stack. My advice: never lock yourself into any of these vendors if you really care about your business and customers. Imagine trying to stay at the frontier and depending on these models. You simply won't be able to. They'll refuse requests (at the model and harness layer), and that will hurt you profoundly. If you run a small research lab, or even plan to do minimal research (we all should be trying to) in the future (with RSI pipelines) for your business, you need to get this part right. Many companies have already realized this and have started building their own intelligence stack. From the harness to training and serving their own models. It's not easy, but it is the way. It's very clear to me that open-source models are truly the only path forward.
As is Gary, Indiana. San Francisco is pretty from above 🥰

By the way, the research that I am talking about is simple research loops (tuning harnesses) for hill climbing. It doesn't even try to train a model or anything. I don't think people realize the implications of this yet. If you plan to participate in a world of RSI, you'll struggle to use these models for anything useful. And this doesn't only apply to research labs; it applies to any business using AI in its products.

What I'm seeing across the industry right now is that the biggest bottleneck to AI adoption isn't model capabilities. It's data infrastructure. Today, we're expanding the Eon Data Foundation with the launch of Eon Yukon, a new serverless data engine purposely built to change that. AI agents need fresh, contextualized data to act. Specialized models need a continuous feed of data and feedback to improve. Both are still served by a stack, an architecture, and methods built for dashboards: -Spark and Flink clusters sized for peak, plus compaction jobs to keep tables usable. -A pipeline and a copy for every consumer, staged bronze to silver to gold. -Hand-written jobs, wired together by an orchestrator and kept alive by specialists. The result: shipping data is complicated, risky, and expensive. While coding agents ship apps in hours, they rarely build or run data pipelines. The data is too volatile, and a mistake costs too much. With Yukon, data moves from ingestion to processing to serving in one continuous flow, without the infrastructure and pipelines traditionally required to connect them. Events become compacted, sorted, deduplicated Iceberg tables within seconds. Real-time aggregations run inline, with fully managed state. Agents and applications can access fresh data with sub-millisecond latency through a Redis-compatible API or through our SQL and spark compatible query engine. Beyond moving and serving data, Yukon makes it continuously understandable - Live column-level statistics, accessible through MCP, give agents visibility into the data. Built-in monitoring, sampling, and data minimization help teams maintain control. At 1M events/sec and equal freshness, Yukon used 4x less compute than Spark and 7x less than Flink. The benchmark is public: run it yourself with Eon’s ingest-bench. This is another major step toward our vision of an Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era, built to both protect enterprise data and unlock its full potential. Media
